did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a call to sing to the Lord a “new song”—an expression emphasizing renewed praise, not merely a repetition of an earlier song. The song is addressed to the “assembly of the faithful.”
Did you know? This verse presents two aspects of the relationship between the people and the Lord: Israel rejoices in its Maker, and the children of Zion rejoice in their King.
Did you know? The praise in this psalm combines movement and musical instruments: dancing, tambourine, and lyre. In this way, it portrays public worship involving singing, music, and joy.

Did you know? The reason for the people’s joy is that the Lord “takes pleasure in his people.” It then says that he “adorns the humble with salvation,” meaning that he grants the humble honor as part of his deliverance.
Did you know? The faithful are described as rejoicing “in glory” and singing for joy even “on their beds.” Their praise is not limited to public gatherings but accompanies them in their rest as well.

Did you know? This verse presents a powerful combination of two symbols: “the high praises of God” in their throats—that is, praise spoken aloud—and a “two-edged sword” in their hands. Words and action thus appear together in the description of the faithful.

Did you know? This verse describes the role of the faithful toward the nations and peoples through two expressions: carrying out vengeance and administering punishment. It places their actions within the context of judgment and conflict.
Did you know? The psalm describes the effect of judgment even on those in positions of power: kings are bound with chains, and nobles with iron fetters.

Did you know? The expression “written judgment” emphasizes that the action described is presented as part of a judgment recorded in advance. The verse concludes by saying that this honor belongs to all his faithful ones, and the psalm returns to the call, “Hallelujah.”
